title: MMORPG Historical Continuation: World and Story

sections.title: Surviving Aza’ra
sections.text:
The MMORPG unfolds after Belavadös has been completely destroyed.
Its absence shapes refugees, laws, routes, labor, and inherited language.
The setting mixes post-apocalyptic survival with working cities rather than depicting an empty wasteland.
Players move among surviving continents, floating settlements and public transit networks.
History can be explored through books, memorials, and stories, but the destroyed continent is never a playable map.
Historical and system reference
The source Steampunk-to-Moonpunk history depicts necessity-driven rebuilding rather than an uninterrupted golden age. Architecture and trade should remember migration, scarcity and displaced communities after Belavadös is destroyed. The continent can be referenced in museums or memories but cannot be traversed.
Next chapter

sections.title: Brassbound Steampunk
sections.text:
The original world document describes the Brassbound Age as industry born from necessity.
Brass, storm-forged metal, pressure conduits and ley-light engineering support homes, tools and transit.
Mechanical systems require fuel, maintenance and safe operating pressure.
Clothes reflect travel and industrial needs, not merely decoration.
Players can build workshops and repair public infrastructure as meaningful professions.
Historical and system reference
The Brassbound Age reference names Zephonara, Emberhold and Vulkiris as industrial cities, alongside brass, storm-forged iron, ley-glass and aether-cable. These are source-backed worldbuilding names, not decorative placeholders. Pressure, repair, fuel and contamination hazards should matter mechanically.
Next chapter

sections.title: Moonpunk Technologies
sections.text:
Later technology uses lunar resonance and refined magical systems to extend the Brassbound infrastructure.
The three moons Duvaen, W’iosamn and Arvalla influence lighting, ritual timing and engineering culture.
Moonpunk vehicles and buildings should still use resources, trained work and physical space.
Digital simulation can treat the three-moon alignment as a calendar condition rather than a free source of limitless power.
Historical and system reference
The three moons are Duvaen, W’iosamn and Arvalla. Lunar resonance can affect ritual timing and machinery as a calendar condition, but Moonpunk technology still needs explicit resources and safeguards. The novel and TTRPG must use the same lunar names.
Next chapter

sections.title: Continents and Boundaries
sections.text:
The surviving setting has different communities in Arzuhan, Dakaroth and Tzaphaer.
Skyborne districts, storm regions, wetlands and industrial cities require distinct travel logic.
Region identifiers are stable across quests, economy and housing.
Belavadös remains a historical name without a traversable destination.
If a map source still shows it, the importer tags that location as retired before gameplay begins.
Next chapter

sections.title: Species and Heritage
sections.text:
Strict species data, legacy race descriptions and mixed communities must be searchable in one place.
The old MMORPG includes 18 named entries but not all are distinct current species.
Ampharils have been merged into Dril’thars.
Kalus’aans and Kalusogals represent mixed ancestry; Azh’raim is an older label to reconcile with Azrahai.
Characters can choose ancestry detail without double-counting species or losing cultural identity.
Historical and system reference
The current strict JSON contains 12 recognized named species, and the older MMORPG contains additional source-backed candidates and mixed groups. The concordance tracks each separately. Ampharils remain Dril'thar heritage, not an independent selectable race. Aza'raans are the hybrid founding people.
Next chapter

sections.title: Careers and Work
sections.text:
Skills, careers and crafting in the original MMORPG support artisans, merchants, archivists, couriers, builders and technical specialists.
Professions require jobs, tools, resources and customers.
A stable task loop includes request, materials, preparation, work, quality check and delivery.
The economy responds to actual completed work, not a simulated paycheck disconnected from the world.
Historical and system reference
Professions can supply restoration, housing, medical services and industry, not only battle bonuses. The original Brassbound text supports work in pressure systems, transit, filters, workshop repairs and magical engineering. Public service jobs can earn rewards without requiring PvP.
Next chapter

sections.title: Housing and Private Dimensions
sections.text:
Players can claim a private dimension and build an entire settlement, including homes, roads, farms, gardens, public services, workshops and meeting places.
Permissions distinguish owner, household, collaborator and visitor.
Every placed object receives a persistent identifier, orientation, size and function.
The dimension may expand, but expansions cost resources and respect adjacency constraints.
This design draws on the user’s requested creative-building scope without copying another game’s assets.
Historical and system reference
Private dimensions should support zoning, roads, workshops, gardens, homes, utilities and visitor permissions. Buildings consume materials and space. The local settlement prototype models a small grid, but a full multiplayer service still requires server authority, permissions and persistence.
Next chapter

sections.title: Terrain and Agriculture
sections.text:
The settlement terrain grid includes soil, water, path, road, garden and natural habitat.
Agriculture requires water, appropriate soil, season and maintenance.
Tree and structure footprints cannot silently overlap.
Regional weather and available labor affect yields.
Players can protect wildlife and build community gardens rather than treating all undeveloped space as empty construction land.
Next chapter

sections.title: Residents and NPC Homes
sections.text:
An NPC resident has a household, occupation, needs, relationships, permissions and schedule.
Their home must be placed before it becomes their address.
A clinic, market or school provides useful settlement services only when staffed and supplied.
NPCs can choose to stay, move or make requests, and the system should remember promises made by players.
Population growth requires infrastructure.
Next chapter

sections.title: Factions and Guilds
sections.text:
Guilds can focus on research, craft, protection, trade, travel, art or community care.
Governance needs clear permissions, resources and member responsibilities.
Reputation depends on decisions, not a single universal good meter.
Historical organizations from the destroyed continent can persist through descendants and archives without surviving as unexplained new cities.
Next chapter

sections.title: Quest and Event Calendar
sections.text:
Events should combine seasonal moon phases with local politics, work orders and natural conditions.
Some activities require a time window, while others stay available to accommodate different schedules.
Quest design permits multiple solutions and stores resulting changes.
Events can spotlight linguistic encounters, refugee histories and recovered documents without inventing a permanent new lore crisis each day.
Next chapter

sections.title: Transportation Network
sections.text:
Skyships, rail, watercraft, road travel and designated short-range portals make exploration possible.
The safest magical jumps terminate at public transit stations.
Unauthorized long-distance jumps expose travelers to serious misarrival risk.
Routes must be verified against world geography and era, with Belavadös unavailable after its destruction.
Vehicles also require accessible boarding, maintenance and storage.
Historical and system reference
Anchored portal stops and maintained sky routes need route metadata, danger states and access restrictions. Destroyed Belavadös cannot appear on current transit menus. Long-range unchecked teleportation is dangerous and must never be the universal default.
Next chapter

sections.title: Economy of Restoration
sections.text:
The post-apocalyptic economy values repair, clean water, safe transit, medical support, housing and salvaged knowledge.
Scarcity has understandable local causes.
A region that rebuilds a bridge can improve trade prices; a broken ferry can isolate a market.
Players should be able to see their contribution to recovery in the physical environment and in residents’ lives.
Next chapter
